nodes.statement: The talk is structured so that the first part defines "radical" and gives evidence for the assumption that computers are a radical novelty, and the second part draws scientific and educational consequences.
nodes.span: The second part of this talk pursues some of the scientific and educational consequences of the assumption that computers represent a radical novelty.
nodes.status_reason: a stated plan of the text, checkable but not derived from anything the reader holds

nodes.statement: People habitually plan for the future using the vocabulary and concepts inherited from past experience, stretching them to fit.
nodes.span: The usual way in which we plan today for tomorrow is in yesterday's vocabulary.
nodes.status_reason: an observation about ordinary practice, checkable against the reader's general experience but not derived

nodes.statement: Linguists observe that word meanings evolve only slowly and gradually.
nodes.span: the meanings of words evolve over time, but also know that this is a slow and gradual process
nodes.status_reason: appeal to linguistic observation; not derivable from held terms

nodes.statement: Coping with novelty by metaphor and analogy works under gradual change but breaks down under sharp discontinuity, where past experience is irrelevant and metaphors mislead.
nodes.span: in the case of a sharp discontinuity, however, the method breaks down
nodes.status_reason: follows from the account of borrowed vocabulary and the slowness of meaning-change in n2 and n3

nodes.statement: A "radical" novelty is defined as one for which the analogical method breaks down.
nodes.span: This is the situation that is characteristic for the "radical" novelty.
nodes.status_reason: definition fixed by the breakdown case identified in n4

nodes.statement: Radical novelty must be approached with a deliberately blank mind, treated as a dissociated topic and learned like a foreign language untranslatable into one's mother tongue.
nodes.span: one has to approach the radical novelty with a blank mind, consciously refusing to try to link it with what is already familiar
nodes.status_reason: follows from n5: if the familiar is inadequate, linking to it must be refused

nodes.statement: Because coping with radical novelty demands hard work, both the adjustment and the novelties themselves are unwelcome.
nodes.span: adjusting to radical novelties is not a very popular activity, for it requires hard work
nodes.status_reason: follows from the effort demanded by the method in n6

nodes.statement: Radical novelties are so disturbing that they tend to be suppressed or ignored, and even the possibility of their existence is commonly denied.
nodes.span: radical novelties are so disturbing that they tend to be suppressed or ignored
nodes.status_reason: extends the unwelcomeness claim n7, and is backed by the historical and contemporary cases that follow

nodes.statement: Gauss suppressed his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry out of fear of the reception it would meet.
nodes.span: he decided to suppress his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry, thus leaving it to Bolyai and Lobatchewsky to receive the flak
nodes.status_reason: historical anecdote offered as evidence; not derived

nodes.statement: The Middle Ages combined rampant reasoning by analogy with near-total intellectual stagnation, and the two go together.
nodes.span: "reasoning by analogy" was rampant; another characteristic was almost total intellectual stagnation
nodes.status_reason: the pairing is explained by n4's account of analogy's failure

nodes.statement: A very large fraction of the population treats gradual change as the only paradigm of history.
nodes.span: the fraction of the population for which gradual change seems to be all but the only paradigm of history is very large
nodes.status_reason: supported only by the author's reported personal observation

nodes.statement: The author's own observation found the number of such people much larger than he had expected.
nodes.span: when I started to observe it, their number turned out to be much larger than I had expected
nodes.status_reason: personal testimony offered as evidence

nodes.statement: The mathematical community tacitly assumes that mathematical activity, teaching and discovery will remain essentially unchanged, as illustrated by Robbins's argument that the human mind is at its capacity limit.
nodes.span: the vast majority of the mathematical community has never challenged its tacit assumption that doing mathematics will remain very much the same
nodes.status_reason: a reported attitude plus a quotation; checkable but not derived

nodes.statement: Robbins escapes the possibility of radical novelty by defining "doing mathematics" so as to exclude any alternative to traditional brain usage.
nodes.span: thus exorcizing the danger of radical novelty by the simple device of adjusting his definitions to his needs
nodes.status_reason: reads Robbins's quoted argument (n13) against the definition of radical novelty n5

nodes.statement: Prevailing educational practice takes almost imperceptible gradual change as its exclusive paradigm, disguising new material as familiar from arithmetic teaching up to tailored calculus courses.
nodes.span: the prevailing educational practice, for which gradual, almost imperceptible, change seems to be the exclusive paradigm
nodes.status_reason: illustrations from ordinary schooling, checkable by the reader but not derived

nodes.statement: An educational practice that fails to prepare the next generation for radical novelties is a serious shortcoming.
nodes.span: I consider the failure of an educational practice to prepare the next generation for the phenomenon of radical novelties a serious shortcoming
nodes.status_reason: follows from n15 together with the need for the special method n6

nodes.statement: Radical novelties matter now because science and technology keep inflicting them while we remain ill-prepared, as relativity, quantum mechanics, the atom bomb and the pill show.
nodes.span: while we are ill-prepared to cope with them, science and technology have now shown themselves expert at inflicting them upon us
nodes.status_reason: combines the unpreparedness claims n8/n11 with cited cases

nodes.statement: Automatic computers embody not one but two radical novelties, and only by identifying them as such can the surrounding mythology be recognized.
nodes.span: automatic computers embody not only one radical novelty but two of them
nodes.status_reason: the central contention, announced here and only argued in the following paragraphs

nodes.statement: We cope with size and complexity by hierarchical decomposition, whose depth is roughly the logarithm of the ratio of the sizes of whole and smallest part.
nodes.span: the depth of a hierarchical decomposition is some sort of logarithm of the ratio of the "sizes" of the whole and the ultimate smallest parts
nodes.status_reason: asserted general principle illustrated by the town example; the logarithm relation is stated, not derived

nodes.statement: Computing spans a size ratio, from bit to hundreds of megabytes and microsecond to half an hour, that utterly baffles the imagination.
nodes.span: From a bit to a few hundred megabytes, from a microsecond to a half an hour of computing
nodes.status_reason: a factual comparison of magnitudes the reader can check from ordinary computing vocabulary

nodes.statement: The first radical novelty is that the programmer alone must bridge this gigantic ratio with one technology, thinking in conceptual hierarchies deeper than any mind faced before.
nodes.span: He has to be able to think in terms of conceptual hierarchies that are much deeper than a single mind ever needed to face before.
nodes.status_reason: follows from the decomposition principle n19 applied to the ratio n20

nodes.statement: The familiar analogy of the computer as a bigger, faster cash register is ridiculously shallow compared with the actual magnitude gap.
nodes.span: the analogy is ridiculously shallow: it is orders of magnitude worse than comparing, as a means of transportation
nodes.status_reason: follows from the ratio in n20 contrasted with the thousand-fold speed ratio cited

nodes.statement: Almost all familiar mechanisms, and our self-image as mechanisms, are analogue: behaviour is a continuous and often monotonic function of parameters.
nodes.span: the vast majority of our mechanisms are viewed as analogue devices whose behaviour is over a large range a continuous function
nodes.status_reason: everyday illustrations (pencil, violin, hammer) checkable by the reader

nodes.statement: The second radical novelty is that the automatic computer is our first large-scale digital device.
nodes.span: The second radical novelty is that the automatic computer is our first large-scale digital device.
nodes.status_reason: contrast with the analogue majority n23 establishes the novelty

nodes.statement: In digitally encoded information the smallest perturbation, a single bit, can have drastic consequences, so no meaningful metric makes small changes give small effects.
nodes.span: there is no meaningful metric in which "small" changes and "small" effects go hand in hand
nodes.status_reason: follows from the digital character n24 contrasted with continuity n23

nodes.statement: Viewing a program as a device analogous to familiar analogue mechanisms is tempting but highly dangerous.
nodes.span: To do so, however, is highly dangerous: the analogy is too shallow because a program is, as a mechanism, totally different
nodes.status_reason: follows from n25's discontinuity together with n23's analogue expectations

nodes.statement: Introducing redundancy or error correction does not essentially change the discontinuity picture.
nodes.span: the picture is not essentially changed by the introduction of redundancy or error correction
nodes.status_reason: asserted parenthetically without argument

nodes.statement: The evidence that computing's novelties are radical will be supplied by explaining a range of otherwise strange phenomena as efforts at hiding or denying the unfamiliar.
nodes.span: I shall do so by explaining a number of otherwise strange phenomena as frantic
nodes.status_reason: a declared argumentative strategy

nodes.statement: "Software Engineering" is a doomed discipline whose de facto charter is "How to program if you cannot", making its goal self-contradictory.
nodes.span: software engineering has accepted as its charter "How to program if you cannot."
nodes.status_reason: an interpretive charge about a field; offered as a phenomenon, not derived

nodes.statement: The choice of the safe, familiar name "engineering" is a primitive naming superstition, shown to be purely symbolic when a manufacturer promoted all its programmers to "software engineers" overnight.
nodes.span: it hired, one night, hundreds of new "software engineers" by the simple device of elevating all its programmers
nodes.status_reason: an anecdote used as illustration of denial

nodes.statement: Measuring programmer productivity as lines of code produced per month reflects the illusion that programs are ordinary devices; lines should be booked as spent, not produced.
nodes.span: we should not regard them as "lines produced" but as "lines spent"
nodes.status_reason: instance of the device-illusion diagnosed in n26

nodes.statement: Quality control by testing persists although it was pointed out two decades ago that testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence.
nodes.span: program testing may convincingly demonstrate the presence of bugs, but can never demonstrate their absence
nodes.status_reason: the persistence is explained as the device-illusion n26 at work

nodes.statement: The term "software maintenance" makes people believe programs and languages wear out, as with the oil company that thought its PASCAL programs did not last.
nodes.span: many people continue to believe that programs —and even programming languages themselves— are subject to wear and tear
nodes.status_reason: another instance of the device analogy n26

nodes.statement: The eager acceptance that software's pains are due to missing "programming tools" rests on an analogy as shallow as medieval reasoning.
nodes.span: the shallowness of the underlying analogy is worthy of the Middle Ages
nodes.status_reason: links the tool metaphor to the analogy failure n4/n26

nodes.statement: The popularity of Artificial Intelligence is explained by the frightening computer becoming less frightening when used to simulate a familiar noncomputer.
nodes.span: the frightening computer becomes less frightening if it is used only to simulate a familiar noncomputer
nodes.status_reason: applies the denial-of-novelty mechanism n8 to a new case, though the author admits it is contested

nodes.statement: All a computer can do is manipulate symbols and produce the results, in a discrete world whose numbers of symbols and manipulations are beyond imagining.
nodes.span: the only thing computers can do for us is to manipulate symbols and produce results of such manipulations
nodes.status_reason: rests on the discreteness n24 and the magnitude claim n20

nodes.statement: A program is best described as an abstract symbol manipulator that becomes concrete when a computer is supplied to it.
nodes.span: the program is an abstract symbol manipulator, which can be turned into a concrete one by supplying a computer
nodes.status_reason: a reformulation warranted by n36's account of what computers do

nodes.statement: It helps to view a program as a formula in a formal system, which puts the programmer's task as deriving that formula and explains why mathematics ignored programming.
nodes.span: It really helps to view a program as a formula.
nodes.status_reason: follows from n37's abstract manipulator, with the two stated benefits as its warrant

nodes.statement: The only reliable way to derive a program is by human symbol manipulation, so we build mechanical symbol manipulators by manipulating symbols ourselves.
nodes.span: We know of only one reliable way of doing that, viz. by means of symbol manipulation.
nodes.status_reason: the uniqueness of the reliable way is asserted, not argued

nodes.statement: Computing science is the study of the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation, which places it beyond formal mathematics and applied logic and makes "automatic programming" a contradiction in terms.
nodes.span: computing science is —and will always be— concerned with the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation
nodes.status_reason: closes the circle drawn by n36, n38 and n39

nodes.statement: In the long run computing science will transcend mathematics and logic by realizing part of Leibniz's Dream of symbolic calculation as an alternative to human reasoning.
nodes.span: by effectively realizing a significant part of Leibniz's Dream of providing symbolic calculation as an alternative to human reasoning
nodes.status_reason: a forward-looking expectation resting on an unheld historical reference

nodes.statement: This vision meets widespread opposition from mathematicians, business, compulsive programmers, computer engineering, the military, the soft sciences and the educational business.
nodes.span: it has met widespread —and sometimes even violent— opposition from all sorts of directions
nodes.status_reason: each listed group's motive is an instance of the denial mechanism n8

nodes.statement: Educational policy is determined almost entirely by extra-scientific circumstances rather than by scientific considerations from the subject taught.
nodes.span: it is hardly influenced by scientific considerations derived from the topics taught, and almost entirely determined by extra-scientific circumstances
nodes.status_reason: asserted diagnosis, illustrated only by rhetorical questions

nodes.statement: Flaherty's statement that the Canadian business elite dismisses academics as irrelevant and powerless illustrates doubts about academic rhetoric's reassuring answers.
nodes.span: the business elite dismisses traditional academics and intellectuals as largely irrelevant and powerless
nodes.status_reason: a quoted external claim used as illustration

nodes.statement: The predicted future of computing science education is business as usual: universities lacking courage to teach hard science and each infantilization of the curriculum hailed as progress.
nodes.span: The universities will continue to lack the courage to teach hard science, they will continue to misguide the students
nodes.status_reason: follows from the extra-scientific determination of policy n43 and the illustration n44

nodes.statement: First suggestion: stop calling a bug a bug and call it an error, which puts blame on the programmer and turns an "almost correct" program into a wrong one.
nodes.span: no longer calling a bug a bug but by calling it an error
nodes.status_reason: follows from the general injunction n6 against misleading familiar metaphors

nodes.statement: Second suggestion: never refer to parts of programs or equipment in anthropomorphic terminology, and forbid students to do so.
nodes.span:
never
 refer to parts of programs or pieces of equipment in an anthropomorphic terminology
nodes.status_reason: an application of the refusal-to-link method n6

nodes.statement: The anthropomorphic metaphor is a handicap that has repeatedly caused avoidable confusion, being both misleading and paralyzing.
nodes.span: the anthropomorphic metaphor —for whose introduction we can blame John von Neumann— is an enormous handicap
nodes.status_reason: grounds the ban n47 in the shallow-analogy diagnosis n26 plus reported experience

nodes.statement: The metaphor is misleading because it treats the unfamiliar discrete in terms of the familiar continuous, and paralyzing because, persons acting in time, it forces operational reasoning about computational behaviours.
nodes.span:
because persons exist and act 
in time
, its adoption effectively prevents a departure from operational semantics
nodes.status_reason: spells out n48 using the discrete/continuous contrast n23-n25

nodes.statement: Operational reasoning is a tremendous waste of mental effort.
nodes.span: This is bad, because operational reasoning is a tremendous waste of mental effort.
nodes.status_reason: asserted here and then argued by the domino example and its transfer to programs

nodes.statement: To demonstrate something about all elements of a large set it is hopelessly inefficient to treat elements individually; the efficient argument uses the set's definition.
nodes.span: the efficient argument does not refer to individual elements at all and is carried out in terms of the set's definition
nodes.status_reason: stated as the point to be illustrated; its warrant is the example that follows

nodes.statement: Define the figure Q as an 8 by 8 square with two opposite 1 by 1 corner squares removed, of area 62, and state the theorem that Q cannot be covered by 31 dominos.
nodes.span:
The theorem is that the figure 
Q
 cannot be covered by 31 of such dominos.
nodes.status_reason: a constructed example, checkable by the reader without domain results

nodes.statement: The theorem can equivalently be stated as: no placement of 31 dominos on adjacent square pairs yields the figure Q.
nodes.span:
no placement of 31 dominos will yield the figure 
Q
nodes.status_reason: a restatement of the construction n52 in placement terms

nodes.statement: One possible proof generates all possible placements and checks each, which is tremendously laborious.
nodes.span: generating all possible placements of dominos and verifying for each placement that it does not yield the figure
nodes.status_reason: the individual-element approach described in n51 applied to n53

nodes.statement: The simple proof colours the squares like a chessboard: each domino covers one white and one black square, but Q's white and black counts differ by two, so no placement yields Q.
nodes.span: each placement covers as many white squares as it covers black squares
nodes.status_reason: argues from the definition of Q n52, exactly as prescribed by n51

nodes.statement: The colouring argument is not only vastly shorter but strictly more powerful, since it proves the generalization to any rectangle with even sides, an infinite family exhaustion cannot handle.
nodes.span: it is also essentially more powerful, for it covers the generalization of
nodes.status_reason: compares n54 with n55 on the generalized case

nodes.statement: The moral is: deal with all elements of a set by ignoring them and working with the set's definition.
nodes.span: deal with all elements of a set by ignoring them and working with the set's definition
nodes.status_reason: generalized from the worked comparison n55-n56, confirming n51

nodes.statement: Since a program defines the set of its possible computations, meeting a specification must be shown by working with the program text while ignoring that it can be executed.
nodes.span: deal with all computations possible under control of a given program by ignoring them and working with the program
nodes.status_reason: the moral n57 applied to the set of computations defined by a program

nodes.statement: A programming language with formal syntax and proof rules is a formal system for which execution is only a model, and formal systems should be treated in their own right, so programs should be reasoned about without mentioning behaviours.
nodes.span: a formal system for which program execution provides only a model
nodes.status_reason: relies on the formal-system/model distinction, which this reader does not hold

nodes.statement: A demonstrated "educational" system visualized features of computations under the student's program, reinforcing precisely what the student must unlearn and thus causing lasting mental damage.
nodes.span: The system highlighted precisely what the student has to learn to ignore, it reinforced precisely what the student has to unlearn
nodes.status_reason: the harm is diagnosed using the ignore-the-computations principle n58

nodes.statement: A program by itself is only half a conjecture; the other half is the functional specification, and the programmer's task is to present such conjectures as proven theorems.
nodes.span: a program is no more than half a conjecture. The other half of the conjecture is the functional specification
nodes.status_reason: follows from the formula view n38 and the specification-as-statement-about-all-computations claim n58

nodes.statement: Curriculum proposal part one: teach predicate calculus as boolean algebra to train manipulation of uninterpreted formulae, renaming {true,false} as {black,white} to sever links to intuition.
nodes.span: To further sever the links to intuition, we rename the values {true, false} of the boolean domain as {black, white}.
nodes.status_reason: implements the blank-mind method n6 and the formula view n38

nodes.statement: Curriculum proposal part two: teach a simple imperative language with few constructs and data types, whose semantics is defined entirely by the accompanying proof rules.
nodes.span: for whatever we introduce, the corresponding semantics is defined by the proof rules that go with it
nodes.status_reason: implements the formal-system view n59 in a teaching language

nodes.statement: Curriculum proposal part three: stress throughout that the programmer's main task is a formal proof that the program meets the formal specification, and use a language not implemented on campus so students cannot test.
nodes.span: we see to it that the programming language in question has not been implemented on campus
nodes.status_reason: follows from n61's proof obligation and n58's injunction to ignore execution

nodes.statement: The objection that the author is out of touch with the real world fails, because real-world problems are mainly those left when effective solutions are refused.
nodes.span: the problems of the real world are primarily those you are left with when you refuse to apply their effective solutions
nodes.status_reason: a rebuttal by assertion rather than by derivation

nodes.statement: The objection that freshmen cannot learn such material is refuted by the fact that since the early 80's such a course has been given successfully to hundreds of freshmen each year.
nodes.span: since the early 80's, such an introductory programming course has successfully been given to hundreds of college freshmen each year
nodes.status_reason: reported experience offered as counter-evidence

nodes.statement: The objection that the course would frustrate students fails, because the manipulation rules are so few and simple that students soon discover a power surpassing their expectations.
nodes.span: the rules of manipulation are in this case so few and simple that very soon thereafter he makes the exciting discovery
nodes.status_reason: rests on the author's teaching experience rather than a derivation

nodes.statement: Universities should welcome rather than fear teaching radical novelties, since this willingness is the main safeguard against dictatorships.
nodes.span: it is their calling to welcome the opportunity to do so
nodes.status_reason: follows from n16's shortcoming charge together with the rewarding results reported
